title: Blocking acrylic and synthetic fibres
subtitle: What works, what doesn't, and when acrylic needs heat to relax
excerpt: Acrylic yarn doesn't respond to water the way wool does. Cold-water spray and wet blocking change very little. To permanently relax and set acrylic, you need steam or heat. The technique is called 'killing' the acrylic — and it's irreversible, so test a swatch first.
sourceNotes: Standard crochet finishing technique. Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book — synthetic fibre care.

glossaryTerms.definition: Applying steam heat to acrylic yarn to permanently break down the fibre structure, relaxing the fabric into a flat, drapey finish. The change is irreversible. Killed acrylic cannot be re-tensioned.
Using a steam iron or garment steamer held just above the surface of an acrylic piece, without direct contact, to relax and set the shape while it is pinned to measurements.

heroPrompt: A small acrylic crochet swatch pinned to a blocking mat, with a steam iron held a few centimetres above the surface — steam just visible between the iron and the swatch. The swatch noticeably flatter on the steamed half than the un-steamed half.

Pin the finished piece to a blocking mat at the correct measurements.
Fill a steam iron with water and set to medium steam. Do not use a dry heat setting.
Hold the iron 3-5 cm above the surface — no contact with the fabric. Pass it slowly across the piece. The steam penetrates the fibres without pressing.
Leave the piece pinned until fully cool and dry. The shape will set as it cools.

attrs.title: Test a swatch first
attrs.body: Killing acrylic is irreversible. A killed acrylic piece is limp and flat — the structure does not recover. Test on a small swatch before applying steam to the finished piece. If the swatch goes limp, you have used too much heat; reduce the steam level or increase the distance.

content.text: Acrylic pieces that don't need blocking

Many acrylic crochet items don't need blocking at all. Amigurumi stuffed shapes: the stuffing holds the shape. Hats with an elastic-stretch fit: blocking isn't needed and may reduce the stretch. Dishcloths and cloths in chunky acrylic: the fabric is already firm and flat from the twist.

A wool/acrylic blend responds to both methods: the wool component responds to water, the acrylic component responds to steam. For most blends, gentle steam blocking at a low-medium setting works well. Check the yarn label for care instructions; the fibre with the lower heat tolerance is the limiting factor.
